## Single-cell RNAseq Workshop {.title-slide}


::: {.subtitle}
Normalization, dimension reduction and clustering
:::

Oct 21, 2026


## Purpose of each step

| Step | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Normalize | Correct library size |
| PCA | Summarize gene variation to fewer dimensions |
| Cluster | Proxy for cell types or states |
| UMAP | Condense expression profiles to a 2D view |



## Begin with raw counts after QC


```{r get_raw}
library(Seurat)
set.seed(42)

seu <- readRDS("/varidata/researchtemp/hpctmp/single_cell_workshop_2026/day2/data/filtered_seu.Rds")

# sort the levels by sample number
seu$orig.ident <- forcats::fct_relevel(seu$orig.ident, function(x) stringr::str_sort(x, numeric=TRUE))

seu

# we 'split' the Seurat object to tell Seurat the cells are derived from different samples
seu[["RNA"]] <- split(seu[["RNA"]], f = seu$orig.ident)
seu
```

Rows represent genes; columns represent cells. Counts are nonnegative and often sparse.

RNA assay: `counts` layer


## Normalization puts cells on a comparable scale

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Problem

One cell has 2,000 detected molecules; another has 10,000. Larger totals can dominate raw comparisons.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### LogNormalize

Divide each gene count by that cell’s total, multiply by 10,000, then apply `log1p`.
:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
`log1p(count / cell total × 10,000)`
:::


## Seurat object structure

```
Seurat object
├── assays slot
│   ├── RNA assay
│   │   └── layers slot
│   │       ├── counts       Raw counts
│   │       ├── data         Normalized expression
│   │       └── scale.data   Scaled expression
├── meta.data slot          Cell annotations and QC metrics
├── reductions slot         PCA, UMAP, etc.
├── graphs slot             Cell–cell graphs (e.g., NN, SNN) for clustering
└── other slots
```

## Run log normalization

```{r normalize}
DefaultAssay(seu) <- "RNA"
seu <- NormalizeData(
  seu,
  normalization.method = "LogNormalize",
  scale.factor = 10000
)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Seurat v5: `seu[["RNA"]]$data`
:::


## Normalization and scaling solve different problems

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### NormalizeData()

Within each cell: correct for differences in total counts and log transform.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### ScaleData()

Within each gene: center values across cells and scale variance before PCA so that highly expressed genes do not dominate.
:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
Scaling never replaces normalization in this standard workflow.
:::




## Focus PCA on informative genes

```{r var_feats}
seu <- FindVariableFeatures(
  seu, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000
)
VariableFeaturePlot(seu)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Highly variable features vary more than expected at their average expression.
:::



## Scale variable genes, then run PCA

```{r pca}
seu <- ScaleData(seu)

seu <- RunPCA(seu, npcs = 50)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Output: `seu[["pca"]]`
:::


## A PC is a weighted pattern of gene expression

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Gene loadings

Which genes contribute to a component? Positive and negative signs describe opposite directions.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Cell scores

Where does each cell fall along that expression pattern?
:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
PCs can correspond to genetic programs of different cell types.
:::



## Inspect the PCs before choosing dimensions

```{r elbow_plot}
ElbowPlot(seu, ndims = 50)
print(seu[["pca"]], dims = 1:5, nfeatures = 5)
DimPlot(seu, reduction = "pca")
```

::: {.takeaway}
Look for diminishing variance and inspect the genes driving each PC.
:::



## Choose PCs for downstream work

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Example choice: PCs 1–30

Use a contiguous range for the tutorial. Record the selected dimension count so results are reproducible.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Sensitivity check

Compare reasonable ranges such as 1–15 and 1–30; inspect whether major groups persist.
:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
Our example: `dims = 1:30`
:::


## Clustering starts with neighbors in PCA space {.compact}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
### FindNeighbors()

Cells near each other in the selected PC dimensions become neighbors.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Shared-neighbor graph

Edges receive stronger support when two cells share many neighbors.
:::

:::

```{r find_neighbors, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
n_pcs <- 30
seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, dims = 1:n_pcs)
```

## Graph communities become cluster labels

- Adjusting the resolution affects the number of clusters returned.
- Multiple cluster resolutions can be specified in the same command.

```{r clusters, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = 0.5, random.seed = 42)
seu$unint_snn <- Idents(seu)

DimPlot(seu, reduction = "pca", group.by = "seurat_clusters")
```

::: {.takeaway}
Higher resolution generally returns more communities; labels are arbitrary IDs.
:::


## UMAP turns local neighbors into a 2D view

![Schematic embedding](img/umap_schematic_embedding.png){.diagram}


::: {.takeaway}
Nearby points often reflect similar profiles in the chosen PCA space.
:::


## Compute and display UMAP

```{r umap, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, dims = 1:n_pcs, seed.use = 42)
DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap", label = FALSE)
FeaturePlot(seu, features = "Sox1")
```

::: {.takeaway}
Clusters were computed from the neighbor graph
:::


## UMAP pictures can change without changing biology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Trust local patterns cautiously

Cells close together tend to have related profiles. Density and relative island spacing can shift.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Verify with expression

Use marker genes, QC metrics, sample labels, and known biology before naming a group.
:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
A cluster boundary on UMAP displays graph labels; clustering uses the neighbor graph.
:::


## Batch correction adds a separate analysis step

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5}
(DimPlot(seu, reduction = "pca", label = FALSE, group.by = "orig.ident") |
  DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap", label = FALSE, group.by = "orig.ident")) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(guides="collect")

```

## Batch correction adds a separate analysis step

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Normalization

Account for count depth within the data.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Integration across batches

Align shared cell populations across technical groups before building a neighbor graph.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Shared cell types should align while meaningful biological differences remain.
:::


## Seurat v5 splits RNA layers by technical group {.dense}

```{r}
# recall this step that we ran at the beginning

# seu[["RNA"]] <- split(seu[["RNA"]], f = seu$orig.ident)

```


::: {.takeaway}
In our dataset, `orig.ident` identifies the sample a given cell came from.
:::


## RPCA integration returns a corrected embedding {.dense}

```{r batch_correct, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
# "For certain functions, each worker needs access to certain global variables. If these are larger than the default limit, you will see this error. To get around this, you can set options(future.globals.maxSize = X), where X is the maximum allowed size in bytes."
options(future.globals.maxSize = 10000 * 1024^2) # 10 GB

seu <- IntegrateLayers(
  object = seu, method = RPCAIntegration,
  orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "integrated.rpca",
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

::: {.takeaway}
The corrected reduction supplies coordinates for the next steps
:::



## Neighbors and UMAP use the integrated reduction {.dense}

```{r integrated_clusters, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
seu <- FindNeighbors(
  seu, reduction = "integrated.rpca", dims = 1:n_pcs
)
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = c(0.3, 0.5, 1), random.seed = 42)
seu <- RunUMAP(
  seu, 
  reduction = "integrated.rpca", 
  dims = 1:n_pcs,
  reduction.name = "umap.integrated", 
  seed.use = 42
)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Both neighbors and UMAP use the same corrected reduction
:::


## Batch mixing and biological signal both matter {.dense}

```{r assess_correction, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap", group.by = "orig.ident")
DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap.integrated", group.by = "orig.ident")

FeaturePlot(seu, 
            reduction = "umap.integrated",
            features = c("Tbx1", "Sox2", "Sox10", "Cdh5"))
```

::: {.takeaway}
Compare mixing within shared cell types and preservation of markers.
:::

Condition comparisons still need sample identities and biological replicates.



## Check correction without erasing biology {.visual-diagnostics}
::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Batch composition
![Compare cluster proportions across batches.](img/batch_composition_diagnostic.png){width=100% height=310 fig-alt="Schematic stacked bars show similar cluster composition versus imbalance across batches."}
Compare cluster percentages across batches. Unequal composition can reflect incomplete correction or real biology; technical replicates should be more similar.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Within-batch structure
![Compare clusters before and after correction within one batch.](img/within_batch_structure_diagnostic.png){width=100% height=310 fig-alt="Schematic overlap heatmaps show preserved clusters versus merged populations within a batch."}
Compare labels within each batch before and after integration. Each corrected cluster should map mainly to one original cluster.
:::

:::

::: {.takeaway}
Good mixing must preserve biological structure. Splitting a cluster may reveal finer structure.
:::

::: {.references}
Schematic examples, not experimental results. Source: [OSCA: Correction diagnostics (Bioconductor 3.21)](https://bioconductor.org/books/3.21/OSCA.multisample/correction-diagnostics.html)
:::

## Save Seurat object for next workshop

```{r save_seu}
saveRDS(seu, "day2_session2_seu.rds")
```


## A complete, runnable Seurat sequence {.dense}

```{r template_code, eval=FALSE}
library(Seurat)
# seu = QC-filtered Seurat object
DefaultAssay(seu) <- "RNA"
seu <- NormalizeData(seu)
seu <- FindVariableFeatures(seu, nfeatures = 2000)
seu <- ScaleData(seu)
seu <- RunPCA(seu, npcs = 50)

seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, dims = 1:30)
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = 0.5)
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, dims = 1:30, seed.use = 42)
```

## A complete, runnable Seurat sequence with integration {.dense}

```{r template_code_integrate, eval=FALSE}
library(Seurat)
# seu = QC-filtered Seurat object
DefaultAssay(seu) <- "RNA"

# specific for integration
seu[["RNA"]] <- split(seu[["RNA"]], f = seu$orig.ident)

seu <- NormalizeData(seu)
seu <- FindVariableFeatures(seu, nfeatures = 2000)
seu <- ScaleData(seu)
seu <- RunPCA(seu, npcs = 50)

# specific for integration
seu <- IntegrateLayers(
  object = seu, method = RPCAIntegration,
  orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "integrated.rpca",
  verbose = FALSE
)

seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, reduction = "integrated.rpca", dims = 1:30)
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = 0.5)
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, reduction = "integrated.rpca", dims = 1:30, seed.use = 42)
```


## Parameters to choose and record {.compact}

| Step | What to record |
|---|---|
| Preprocessing | LogNormalize or SCT v2 |
| PCA | Selected genes and number of PCs |
| Integration | Technical grouping, method |
| Clustering | PC range, resolution, seed |
| UMAP | Reduction, PC range, seed and settings |


## Takeaways {.summary}

1. LogNormalize adjusts cell totals.
2. PCA captures major gene expression patterns.
3. Integration aligns shared populations across batches.
4. Clustering groups cells on a neighbor graph.
5. UMAP displays relationships in two dimensions.

## Bonus: Try other integration methods

- Note how these are stored as additional reduction objects.

- These can each be used for clustering and UMAP by specifying the relevant reduction in the 'reduction' arguments of FindNeighbors() and RunUMAP().

```{r more_integrations, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}

seu <- IntegrateLayers(object = seu, 
                        method = HarmonyIntegration, 
                        orig.reduction = "pca",
                        new.reduction = "integrated.harmony", 
                        verbose = FALSE)

# need to load this package to get FastMNNIntegration
library(SeuratWrappers)
seu <- IntegrateLayers(object = seu, 
                        method = FastMNNIntegration, 
                        new.reduction = "integrated.mnn",
                        verbose = FALSE)
    
seu@reductions
```


## Bonus: Try scTransform instead of NormalizeData(), FindVariableFeatures(), and ScaleData()

SCTransform models the raw UMI counts

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Gene-wise count model

Fits regularized negative-binomial models to account for sequencing depth.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Variance-stabilized residuals

Pearson residuals describe expression above or below each gene’s fitted expectation.
:::

:::

::: {.takeaway}
Seurat v5 uses SCT v2 by default
:::

## Bonus: Try scTransform instead of NormalizeData(), FindVariableFeatures(), and ScaleData()

First, make a new copy of the Seurat object with just the raw counts and meta data.

```{r sctransform_prep, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
# Rejoin the RNA layers so that GetAssayData can work; also needed for downstream analyses like DE analysis.
seu <- JoinLayers(seu, assay = "RNA")

counts <- GetAssayData(seu, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")

seu_sct <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts,
  meta.data = seu[[]][colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE],
  assay = "RNA"
)

seu_sct[["RNA"]] <- split(seu_sct[["RNA"]], f = seu_sct$orig.ident)
```

## Bonus: Try scTransform instead of NormalizeData(), FindVariableFeatures(), and ScaleData()

- seu[["SCT"]]$scale.data: Contains the Pearson residuals used directly as input for PCA.
- seu[["SCT"]]$counts: Contains the 'corrected' UMI counts (expected counts if all cells had uniform sequencing depth).
- seu[["SCT"]]$data: Contains the log-normalized version of the corrected counts for visualization (e.g., FeaturePlots, ViolinPlots).

```{r sctransform_workflow, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE}
seu_sct <- SCTransform(seu_sct)
seu_sct # note new SCT assay is now the active assay
seu_sct <- RunPCA(seu_sct, npcs = 30)
seu_sct <- IntegrateLayers(object = seu_sct, method = RPCAIntegration, normalization.method = "SCT", new.reduction = "rpca.sct")
seu_sct <- FindNeighbors(seu_sct, dims = 1:30, reduction = "rpca.sct")
seu_sct <- FindClusters(seu_sct, resolution = 2)

seu_sct
```
